Promoting the long-tenured, well-liked candidate would not align with the value placed on merit and achievement. Therefore, the manager should choose the candidate with exceptional technical skills.

In the United States, bringing up a problem by implying a character flaw is not the usual way to handle it. The expectation is to discuss the issue in a specific way that does not suggest anything about the person's character. So the colleague should point out the specific errors in the report without implying that the person who prepared it is careless. This approach keeps the focus on the work itself and avoids making the other person feel personally attacked. It is more likely to lead to a constructive conversation and a solution.

In South Africa, a host's invitation to 'stay as long as you like' is not a literal permission to remain indefinitely. It is a polite gesture, and the guest is expected to read the situation and leave at a reasonable time. When the host glances at the clock, that is a clear signal that the visit has run long enough. The guest should therefore take the hint and leave promptly. Staying longer would ignore the host's nonverbal cue and could make the host uncomfortable. The appropriate action is to thank the host and depart.

In Argentina, the idea that extended families are not expected to regularly visit each other or celebrate major occasions together is mistaken. Maintaining close relationships and shared traditions with extended family is important there, so relatives are expected to visit one another regularly and to celebrate major occasions together. For a young couple who has just moved to a new neighborhood, this expectation applies especially to a major holiday approaching. They should visit their relatives for the holiday, because doing so honors the close family bonds and shared traditions that are valued in Argentina. Not visiting would go against the common expectation of staying connected with extended family during important celebrations.

In Ethiopia, the idea that the eldest son should pursue his own independent life and leave household leadership to the mother or other relatives is not the usual expectation. When a father passes away, the eldest son is commonly expected to take on the role of head of the household. This means he is responsible for supporting his mother and younger siblings, making decisions for the family, and maintaining the household. In this situation, the eldest son should step into that leadership role rather than leaving it to others. Pursuing his own independent life would be seen as neglecting his duty to his family. Therefore, the eldest son is expected to take on the role of head of the household.

In the Netherlands, a decision is not simply made and left behind when the discussion has not been all-inclusive, structured, and detailed. The expectation is that if some members have not yet voiced their opinions, the team should not proceed with a decision. Instead, the team should continue the discussion until every member has had a chance to contribute. This ensures that the decision is well-considered and that no one feels excluded. Therefore, the team should keep talking until all members have voiced their opinions, rather than moving on to the next meeting.

In New Zealand, letting friends pay for you repeatedly without reciprocating is not seen as harmless; it can damage your reputation. Protecting one's public image and avoiding the appearance of taking advantage of others matters there. People generally expect that if friends have covered the cost several times, the person will make an effort to pay for the next outing. The person should therefore pay for the upcoming outing themselves. This shows they are not taking advantage of their friends' generosity and helps maintain a good standing among them.

In Ethiopia, repeating a compliment about a child after the parent has acknowledged it is not the usual polite practice. The common expectation is to avoid saying the same praise more than once, because doing so can be seen as tempting fate or inviting the evil eye. After the friend has thanked the guest, the guest should stop complimenting the child and move on to another topic. Continuing to admire the child would go against this preference and could make the parent uncomfortable. So the guest should not repeat the compliment or keep focusing on the child.

In Ethiopia, declining a second serving with a direct and firm refusal without any bow is not the usual way to handle this. When a guest cannot accept more food, the expected gesture is to bow the head while declining. This bow signals respect and acknowledges the host's generosity, even when the guest is full. So the guest should bow their head while politely declining the second serving. A direct, firm refusal without a bow could come across as abrupt or lacking in courtesy, whereas the bow softens the refusal and shows appreciation for the offer.

In Japan, the idea that the most senior person simply takes the first sip without any toast is not how a dinner party usually begins. The customary practice is for everyone to wait until the most senior person offers a toast, typically saying 'kanpai,' and then all raise their glasses together. This shared toast marks the start of drinking and shows respect for the group and the occasion. So in this situation, the colleagues should wait for the senior person to propose the toast, then everyone drinks at the same time. Taking the first sip without a toast would miss the communal and respectful gesture that is expected.

In Russia, a personal friendship with a key decision-maker is not something to keep out of a business negotiation; it is a legitimate channel to help move things forward. The claim that personal business relationships should not be used to influence negotiations misreads how such ties are commonly treated there. When talks stall, it is expected that one can draw on that personal connection to help resolve the impasse. The partner should ask the close friend to intervene and help resolve the negotiation deadlock. This fits the situation because the friendship is already established and the talks have been stuck for weeks, so a personal appeal is a natural way to break the logjam. Avoiding the friendship and sticking only to professional merits would ignore a resource that is normally available and could leave the deadlock unresolved.

In Germany, the expectation that children stay with their parents until marriage or starting a family is not the usual one. Once a young adult has completed vocational training and has a stable income, most people would be expected to move out and live independently. The situation described fits this pattern: the person is financially self-sufficient and no longer needs parental support. Therefore, the young adult would be expected to find their own apartment and live independently. Continuing to live with parents despite being able to support oneself would not align with the common expectation of establishing an independent household at this stage.

In Russia, the gesture described is not seen as harmless or playful. Placing the wrist on the inside of the opposite elbow and bending the elbow with a closed fist is commonly understood as a rude or offensive sign. It is not a casual or friendly movement, so a person making it during a conversation would likely be perceived as disrespectful. The appropriate interpretation is that the gesture is rude or offensive, not playful.

In the United Kingdom, when a new member's name is announced to a group, the expectation is not that others will introduce themselves by name. Instead, the new member is expected to take the initiative and introduce themselves to the other attendees. This means the new member should approach people and offer their name, rather than waiting for others to do so. In this situation, the new member should introduce themselves to the other attendees. Waiting for others to introduce themselves would be seen as passive and might hinder the networking process.

In Greece, when waiting in a queue, it is commonly expected that a person keeps their belongings from touching the person in front or behind them. This expectation reflects a concern for avoiding actions that may cause discomfort or offense to others. In this situation, the backpack occasionally touching the person in front would likely be seen as rude. The person in front would probably interpret the contact as a lack of consideration for their personal space. Therefore, the person in front would most likely view the backpack touching them as rude rather than acceptable.

In Sri Lanka, finishing all the food on one's plate is not the usual way to signal that one does not want a second serving. In some households, the common expectation is the opposite: leaving a small amount of food on the plate shows that the guest is satisfied and does not wish for more. Therefore, the guest should leave a small amount of food on the plate. This action communicates fullness and contentment without needing to speak. Finishing everything might be interpreted as still being hungry or wanting another serving, which would not match the guest's intention.

In Portugal, the idea that grandparents generally do not move into the same home to help with childcare is not accurate. It is common for grandparents to live with the family and take on a significant role in caring for the grandchildren. Given that both parents work full-time and the grandparents are considering moving closer, a customary arrangement would be for the grandparents to move into the same home as the couple and their children. This allows them to provide daily childcare support and be closely involved in the children's upbringing. Living separately and helping from a distance would be less typical in this context, as the expectation is often for grandparents to be part of the household when they are able to assist.

In Sudan, the left hand is not treated as equally acceptable for eating. The common expectation is that the left hand is reserved for cleaning and is considered unclean, so it should not be used to take food from a shared platter. The guest should therefore use the right hand to take food. Using the left hand would be seen as inappropriate in this setting. The right hand is the proper choice for handling food when eating with a host.

In Samoa, simply saying "excuse me" without any bow is not the usual way to excuse oneself for obstructing someone's view. The common expectation is to accompany the apology with a slight bow. So when the person pauses in front of someone and blocks their view, they should say "excuse me" while bowing slightly. This shows respect and acknowledges the inconvenience caused. A bow alone, without words, would not be enough; the verbal apology is part of the gesture. Therefore, the person is expected to say "excuse me" while bowing slightly.

In Cyprus, calling a colleague a 'tzampatzis' after they forgot their wallet is not usually taken as a light-hearted joke. The term carries a strong negative connotation, implying that the person is a free rider or someone who takes advantage of others. In this situation, the colleague who forgot their wallet is being accused of deliberately avoiding payment, which is a serious accusation. Therefore, the remark would most likely be perceived as a serious insult, not as playful teasing. It would be better to handle the situation with understanding, perhaps by offering to cover the cost this time, rather than using a derogatory label.

In Sri Lanka, when a mutual acquaintance introduces two people, it is generally considered rude for one person to ask the acquaintance questions about the other person while that person is standing there. The person being introduced would likely interpret the question as rude, because it suggests a lack of direct engagement and can feel like being discussed behind one's back, even in a brief moment. The expectation is to address the person directly rather than inquire about them through the introducer. Therefore, the person being introduced would probably feel uncomfortable or disrespected by the question.

In Canada, a calm and fact-based response to a controversial topic is not what makes someone less likely to continue the discussion. On the contrary, when the other person stays respectful and brings in relevant facts and studies, the first colleague is more likely to keep the conversation going. The expectation is that a respectful, intellectually informed exchange encourages further discussion rather than shutting it down. So in this situation, the first colleague is more likely to continue discussing the topic because the other person remains respectful and intellectually informed about the subject.

In Russia, a deadlock in negotiations is not usually met with a quick move toward compromise. The expectation is that both sides will hold their positions and wait for the other to show flexibility first. So one partner should expect the other to remain firm and let the impasse stand, rather than offering a middle ground. This is because the common practice is to wait it out, not to seek a compromise. Therefore, the partner should not anticipate a concession; instead, they should be prepared for a prolonged standoff until one side eventually yields.

In Cyprus, the idea that people are more willing to engage in business deals with those offering the best terms, regardless of personal relationship, does not reflect the usual preference. Reliability and trustworthiness in close relationships are important, so business owners often prefer to work with those they know and trust. A long-time acquaintance with whom the owner has a personal relationship is seen as more dependable than a new company, even if the new company offers a slightly better price. Therefore, the business owner is more likely to choose the long-time acquaintance. Choosing the new company based only on price would overlook the value placed on established trust and personal connection in Cypriot business dealings.

In the Philippines, the idea that a young adult should keep the bond with aunts and uncles weaker than the bond with parents does not reflect the usual expectation. Maintaining close relationships with extended family members is important there, and this includes aunts and uncles. People are encouraged to make the relationship with aunts and uncles as strong as the relationship with parents. So during a family gathering, the young adult should spend time with the aunt and uncle in a way that shows the same closeness and care as with the parents. Treating the aunt and uncle as less important would go against the value placed on close extended family ties.

In Türkiye, a single offer close to the bottom-line figure is not the usual way to negotiate. The common expectation is to make several offers, each moving gradually toward the final price, because prices often shift by a large percentage between the initial offer and the final decision. The buyer should therefore make several offers, each moving gradually toward the final price. This approach fits the situation because it allows the negotiation to progress through multiple rounds, which is how prices are typically adjusted there. Making only one offer near the bottom line would likely be seen as too abrupt and could miss the opportunity to reach a mutually acceptable price through the expected back-and-forth.

In Vietnam, asking a new colleague about marital status and salary during a coffee break is not the usual way to get to know someone. Such personal questions are generally considered inappropriate in a workplace setting, especially with someone you have just met. The expectation is to keep the conversation light and professional, avoiding topics that could make the other person uncomfortable. Therefore, the coworker should not ask about marital status or salary. Instead, they might talk about work, hobbies, or other neutral topics. This approach respects the new colleague's privacy and helps build a comfortable working relationship.

In Japan, leaving a small amount of food on the plate is not the usual way to signal satisfaction and a lack of desire for more food. The common expectation is that a guest who has finished eating and does not want more should leave the plate empty. An empty plate shows that the meal was enjoyed and that the guest is full. Therefore, the guest should leave the plate empty to indicate satisfaction and no desire for more food. Leaving a small amount of food could be seen as a sign that the guest was not fully satisfied or that they want more.

In Russia, relying only on a face-to-face meeting and skipping a follow-up is not how business relationships are usually kept warm. The common expectation is that a person should follow up after a meeting to maintain the warmth of the business relationship. So the partner should send a follow-up message summarizing the discussion and next steps. This keeps the connection alive and shows that the meeting mattered. Not sending anything could make the other partner feel the relationship is not being taken seriously.

In Australia, the idea that business relationships should remain strictly professional and avoid personal friendships is not the usual expectation. People there commonly value maintaining long-term relationships and loyalty, so a sales representative who has worked with a client for years is expected to invest in the relationship beyond transactions. Building a personal connection, such as through a casual lunch, is seen as a natural way to strengthen trust and dependability. Therefore, the sales representative should invite the client to a casual lunch to build a personal friendship. Keeping the relationship strictly professional would miss the opportunity to deepen the bond that Australians typically appreciate in long-term business dealings.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina, arriving empty-handed to a colleague's home for a first dinner party is not the usual expectation. When invited to someone's house for a social occasion or visiting for the first time, it is common to bring a small gift as a gesture of appreciation. Suitable gifts include flowers, sweets, or alcohol. Therefore, the person should bring a small gift such as flowers, sweets, or alcohol. This shows thoughtfulness and respect for the host's hospitality. Going without a gift might be seen as less considerate in this context.

In Ethiopia, a response like "let me think about that" is not usually a sign that the person is genuinely undecided and needs time to consider. Instead, it is commonly understood as a polite way of declining the request. The colleague should therefore interpret the team member's response as a refusal to take on the additional project. This indirect style of communication helps avoid direct confrontation or embarrassment, so the colleague should not press for a more definite answer. The appropriate interpretation is that the team member is declining the request.

In India, a new employee is not expected to speak in a direct, frank manner with colleagues they have not worked with before. The usual expectation is to be indirect and polite, especially when raising a concern. So the new employee should phrase the concern about the timeline in a gentle, indirect way, perhaps by asking a question or suggesting an alternative rather than stating the flaw outright. This approach fits the situation because it respects the lack of a strong relationship and avoids putting colleagues on the spot. Speaking directly and frankly would feel too blunt and could be seen as disrespectful in this context.

In India, a business partner is not expected to stick rigidly to the terms discussed in a meeting when they have the chance to consult their manager. The common expectation is that a representative may adjust their position between meetings after checking with their superior. Here, the supplier's representative has the opportunity to speak with their manager before the next meeting, so they should do so and then adjust their position based on the manager's guidance. This fits the situation because the representative is not locked into the earlier terms; they can refine their stance after internal consultation. Adhering strictly to the original terms would miss the chance to align with the manager's input, which is a normal part of the process.

In Russia, the idea that it is equally acceptable for men and women to be unshaved, slightly unkempt, and out of shape does not reflect the usual expectation. There is a common preference for women to maintain a more groomed appearance, especially in social settings like a family gathering. A woman with uncombed hair and a loose, casual outfit is more likely to be seen as not meeting that standard, whereas a man who is unshaved and in casual clothes is generally given more leeway. Therefore, the man's appearance is more acceptable at the gathering. This is not a strict rule, but a widely held expectation about how men and women are judged on their presentation.

In Israel, the expectation that everyone, including upper management, arrives at a meeting on time or slightly early is not the usual practice. It is common for senior managers to arrive late to meetings, and this is generally accepted as part of the workplace culture. Therefore, the senior manager's arrival after 10:15 AM is most likely seen as a normal occurrence rather than a sign of disrespect or poor planning. The team would probably not interpret the lateness as a problem, but rather as a typical behavior for someone in a senior position.

In Japan, the claim that the highest-ranking person sits closest to the door is not how seating is usually arranged in a large meeting. The common practice is for colleagues from the same company to sit on the same side of the table, but the highest-ranking person takes the seat farthest from the door. This placement gives the senior person the most secure and honored position, away from the entrance. Therefore, the colleagues should sit on the same side of the table, with the highest-ranking person farthest from the door. Sitting with the highest-ranking person closest to the door would reverse the expected order and could be seen as a mistake in showing proper respect.

In Russia, a seating arrangement or speaking order is not something a person may simply ignore. Following formal procedures and rules is important there, so the employee is expected to respect the order of seating or speaking. The name cards indicate where each person should sit, and the junior employee should take the seat indicated by their name card. Sitting wherever they prefer would disregard the established order and could be seen as failing to follow the meeting's formal structure. Therefore, the employee should follow the seating arrangement and sit in the seat indicated by their name card.

In Sudan, the idea that extended families in urban areas commonly live in separate single-family homes is not accurate. A customary arrangement is for the extended family to share a multi-storey house, with each nuclear family occupying a separate floor. For this married couple with two children, that means living in a multi-storey house where the husband's parents and his brother's family each have their own floor. This arrangement keeps the extended family close while giving each nuclear family its own space. Choosing separate single-family homes would go against this common practice.

In Tonga, a 15-minute delay to a prearranged meeting is not usually read as a sign that the other person is disregarding the agreed time. The common expectation is that meeting times and opening hours are not strictly observed, so a short delay is generally seen as normal rather than as a breach of punctuality. The waiting colleague should therefore interpret the delay as a routine part of how time is handled in Tongan business settings, not as a personal slight or a sign of disrespect. Treating it as a serious violation would misread the local practice and could create unnecessary tension between colleagues.

In Mexico, the idea that independent adults generally avoid location-sharing features to protect their privacy does not reflect the common practice. Many adult siblings there do use such systems, not to invade privacy but to stay connected and know when the other is safe. The customary thing for these siblings would be to enable the location-sharing feature so they can see each other's real-time location and receive automatic notifications when the other arrives home. This fits the situation because they live in different parts of the same city and have smartphones, making it easy to share location. Choosing not to enable it would miss a common way for family members to keep in touch and feel reassured about each other's well-being.

In New Zealand, a marae is not a place where a group without a male or a Te Reo Māori speaker can simply attend without prior contact. The expectation is that the group should contact the marae beforehand to arrange for a male and a Te Reo Māori speaker to accompany them. This is because the marae's protocols require someone to speak on behalf of the visitors, and the absence of a male or a fluent speaker would leave the group unable to participate properly in the welcome. Therefore, the group should reach out to the marae in advance to make these arrangements. Attending without doing so would be seen as failing to respect the marae's customs and could cause discomfort for the hosts.

In Russia, the gesture described is not read as a friendly sign of approval. The 'Okay' symbol, with the forefinger and thumb forming a circle and the other fingers stretched out, is commonly understood there as a rude or obscene gesture. A local vendor at a market would likely interpret it as offensive rather than as a request for attention or a sign of agreement. The tourist should avoid using this gesture, as it could cause offense or be seen as disrespectful. Instead, a simple wave or a verbal call would be more appropriate for getting the vendor's attention.

In North Macedonia, the seating arrangement described is not the usual one for a formal family dinner. The head of the family is expected to sit in the middle of one side of the table, with the godmother and godfather seated on either side of them. This places the godmother and godfather next to the head of the family, not at the opposite end. Therefore, the head of the family should sit in the middle of one side of the table, with the godmother and godfather seated on either side of them. This arrangement keeps the godmother and godfather close to the head of the family, which is the common expectation in this setting.
